title: Seinfeld Stopped Airing Nearly 30 Years Ago; Its Copyright Revenue Is Now Over $7 Billion
dek: A 1970s rule that prohibited TV networks from holding financial equity in programs let production companies capture nearly all long-term revenue—a comedy that cost $250 million to produce has become a copyright asset that can still generate another $1 billion per decade.
why: A deep look at how a sitcom that stopped airing thirty years ago became Hollywood's most durable copyright money-printing machine—not because of the content itself, but because of its ownership structure.
who: Founders, investors, and anyone concerned with how content copyright economics, ownership structures, and streaming monetization work—plus anyone trying to understand how Hollywood deal-making actually functions.

points.h: The show's concept came from convenience-store small talk
points.body: In November 1988, after meeting Larry at Catch a Rising Star, Jerry and he walked into a Korean convenience store on the Upper East Side and joked about products on the shelves. Larry said on the spot, ‘This is it—this is what our show should be like.’ The following night at Westway Diner, Jerry raised the question ‘Most people ask where you get your material from,’ and the two decided to make that question itself the show's premise. The show didn't start in a pitch meeting—it started from two stand-up comedians shooting the breeze.

points.h: ‘No hugs, no learning’ denied an entire genre
points.body: Before Seinfeld, every sitcom relied on character growth and emotional arcs to move audiences—like Full House, where the dad sits on the bed and teaches his daughter life lessons. Seinfeld did the opposite: do something wrong, get caught, lie, dig an even deeper hole, and learn nothing. It stripped away all the moral commitment and emotional-repair obligations of traditional sitcom, clearing the ground for pure joke work. This wasn't just a funny premise; it was heretical to the entire TV comedy genre.

points.h: A forgotten rule transformed production companies into startups
points.body: The 1970 Fin-Syn rule barred TV networks from owning the financial equity in programs; all long-term value went to production companies. Networks typically paid only 60% to 80% of production costs—production companies bore the risk—but in exchange, production companies got all future revenue: international rights, syndication, ancillaries. This created a Silicon Valley-style startup ecosystem: most shows fail, but the ones that succeed do so extremely well. Networks ran a short-term rental business; production companies ran a long-term ownership business.

points.h: A modest stake negotiated in a risky deal turned into hundreds of millions
points.body: Jerry and Larry each owned 15% of the show. According to reports, the split was roughly: Sony as distributor ~15%, Jerry and Larry ~15% each, agents ~5%, Castle Rock and its successors ~50%. Because the show ultimately generated billions in revenue, the equity stake the two creators negotiated back then eventually converted into hundreds of millions in long-term payoffs.

points.h: Thursday's advertising revenue exceeded every other day of the week combined
points.body: When asked why Thursday night was so important, David's answer was direct: Thursday's ad revenue exceeded all other weekdays combined. It wasn't a content difference—it was an advertising-market difference. Thursday is the last window for ad buyers pushing weekend consumption and Friday movie promotions. NBC's Thursday lineup earned more than any single other day of the week, so when Seinfeld moved from Wednesday to Thursday, it didn't just get a bigger stage—it entered a completely different commercial tier.

points.h: He turned down $110 million to leave while the audience was still cheering
points.body: In late 1997, GE CEO Jack Welch personally took Jerry to brunch and offered $110 million—22 episodes at $5 million each, five times Jerry's record salary. Jerry refused and announced the show's end at Christmas. His reasoning: a stand-up comedian's philosophy is to exit while the audience is still screaming, so they'll remember you forever. The subsequent three decades of rising copyright licensing prices seemed to validate that judgment.

points.h: A $250 million investment keeps generating $1 billion per decade
points.body: Total production cost was approximately $250 million. Since 1998, not a dime more went in. The next thirty years were pure revenue: ads, syndication, DVD, streaming—over $7 billion cumulative, and still counting $1 billion per decade. The costs were paid off thirty years ago. This is an asset class where you invest one dollar and it generates interest for thirty years straight—not a one-shot content business.

points.h: Reruns, not the original broadcast, kept the show alive for decades
points.body: 2021 Nielsen data showed that 41% of the audience at that time were either infants when it ended or not yet born. The show wasn't living off nostalgia for the original audience; instead, it passed to a new generation through sheer ubiquity, creating a self-reinforcing cycle: more broadcasts meant higher familiarity, higher viewership meant higher licensing fees, and higher fees bought more broadcasts. The show's long life wasn't built on sentiment—it was built on being everywhere.
